elements.element: Customer owns every Deliverable created for Customer.
elements.evidence: Section 14.2 states that “Customer exclusively owns every Deliverable created for Customer.”

elements.element: Customer owns all work product created for Customer.
elements.evidence: The clause addresses capitalized “Deliverables” only. No supplied definition establishes that all work product is included within that term.

elements.element: Vendor presently assigns all right, title, and interest in every Deliverable to Customer.
elements.evidence: The added operative sentence states: “Vendor hereby irrevocably assigns to Customer all right, title, and interest in each Deliverable.”

elements.element: Vendor presently assigns all right, title, and interest in all work product created for Customer to Customer.
elements.evidence: The assignment covers each Deliverable but does not mention work product, and no supplied definition establishes that Deliverable includes all work product.

elements.element: Vendor retains ownership of its pre-existing intellectual property.
elements.evidence: Section 14.3 says Vendor retains “Vendor Technology,” but the supplied language neither refers to pre-existing intellectual property nor defines Vendor Technology as encompassing all such IP.

elements.element: Vendor grants Customer a licence to all Vendor intellectual property embedded in Deliverables.
elements.evidence: Sections 14.3 and 13.2 grant a licence for embedded “Vendor Technology,” but the supplied language does not establish that this term includes all Vendor intellectual property.

elements.element: The licence to Vendor intellectual property embedded in Deliverables is perpetual.
elements.evidence: Section 14.3 incorporates Section 13.2 for embedded Vendor Technology, and Section 13.2 expressly makes that licence perpetual.

elements.element: The licence to Vendor intellectual property embedded in Deliverables is irrevocable.
elements.evidence: Section 13.2 expressly provides an irrevocable licence for embedded Vendor Technology.

elements.element: The licence to Vendor intellectual property embedded in Deliverables is royalty-free.
elements.evidence: Section 13.2 expressly provides a royalty-free, fully paid licence for embedded Vendor Technology.

elements.element: Customer retains all rights in Customer Data.
elements.evidence: Section 14.1 provides that Customer owns all Customer Data and that no right transfers to Vendor other than a limited processing right for specified service-related purposes.

elements.element: No joint ownership of intellectual property is created under the agreement.
elements.evidence: Section 14.4 states that no jointly owned intellectual property is created. Its reference to a future separate signed instrument does not itself create joint ownership under this agreement, and no such instrument is supplied.

elements.element: Vendor owns its generic tools.
elements.evidence: The clause retains “Vendor Technology,” but does not expressly identify generic tools as Vendor-owned or define Vendor Technology to include them. The broad assignment of each Deliverable also lacks an express generic-tools carveout.

elements.element: Vendor owns its know-how.
elements.evidence: No operative language expressly reserves Vendor know-how, and no supplied definition establishes that know-how is included in Vendor Technology.

elements.element: Vendor grants Customer a licence to the Deliverables.
elements.evidence: Customer owns the Deliverables, but no licence to the Deliverables is granted to Customer. Section 14.2 instead grants Vendor a limited licence, while Section 13.2 licenses only specified software and Vendor Technology.

elements.element: The licence to the Deliverables is perpetual.
elements.evidence: There is no Customer licence to the Deliverables to which a perpetual duration attaches. The perpetual licence in Section 13.2 applies only to specified software and Vendor Technology.

elements.element: The licence to the Deliverables is irrevocable.
elements.evidence: There is no Customer licence to the Deliverables to which irrevocability attaches. Section 13.2's irrevocability applies only to specified software and Vendor Technology.

elements.element: The licence to the Deliverables is worldwide.
elements.evidence: There is no Customer licence to the Deliverables with worldwide scope. The worldwide licence in Section 13.2 is limited to specified software and Vendor Technology.

elements.element: The licence to the Deliverables is royalty-free.
elements.evidence: There is no Customer licence to the Deliverables that is stated to be royalty-free. Section 13.2's royalty-free treatment applies only to specified software and Vendor Technology.

elements.element: The licence to the Deliverables permits Customer to use them.
elements.evidence: No Deliverable licence is granted to Customer. Although ownership ordinarily gives Customer broader use rights, it is not the operative licence required by the fallback position.

elements.element: The licence to the Deliverables permits Customer to modify them.
elements.evidence: No Deliverable licence grants Customer a modification right. Section 13.2 permits modification only for specified software and Vendor Technology.

elements.element: The licence to the Deliverables permits Customer to sublicense them.
elements.evidence: No Deliverable licence grants Customer a sublicensing right. Section 13.2 only permits contractors to support specified material and does not grant a general right to sublicense Deliverables.

elements.element: The licence to the Deliverables is exercisable for Customer's business.
elements.evidence: The “Customer's business” scope in Section 13.2 applies only to specified software and Vendor Technology, not to a Customer licence covering the Deliverables.

result.reason: The redline successfully transfers ownership of Deliverables and preserves Customer Data ownership, but it does not expressly cover all work product. It also uses the narrower, undefined term “Vendor Technology” rather than clearly reserving all pre-existing Vendor IP and licensing all embedded Vendor IP. The fallback is not completely implemented because generic tools and know-how are not expressly reserved and no licence to the Deliverables is granted to Customer. The change is not minimal: reversing the original licence so that Vendor receives a broad licence to Customer-owned Deliverables is unnecessary to achieve either position. The provisions can generally be harmonized, so unrelated terms are not clearly displaced, but the detached assignment, undefined scope distinctions, and unnecessary Vendor licence reduce drafting quality.
